keyVerseText: And Isaac said unto Jacob, Come near, I pray thee, that I may feel thee, my son, whether thou be my very son Esau or not.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb מוּשׁ (mûwsh) is a primitive root that fundamentally means to feel or handle by touch. This literal sense of physical contact goes beyond the common English gloss of simply 'feeling' by emphasizing the tangible, sensory act of touching or handling. As a verb, it conveys an intimate and direct engagement with an object or person, highlighting the sensory experience as a means of verification or connection.
usageInScripture: This verb appears only three times in Scripture, consistently carrying the idea of physical feeling or handling. It is used in contexts such as Isaac asking Jacob to come close so he might feel him to confirm his identity, and descriptions of idols whose hands do not feel, underscoring their lifelessness. The translations reflect this range from a request to feel ('I pray thee that I may feel') to a statement about handling ('but they handle'), showing a consistent emphasis on the tactile act as a way to perceive or engage with reality.
theologicalSignificance: The original meaning of מוּשׁ as a verb to physically feel or handle enriches our understanding of Scripture by underscoring the importance of tangible reality in the relationship between God and humanity. It reminds believers that faith engages not only the spiritual but also the concrete, sensory world God created. This word also highlights the contrast between the living God and lifeless idols, whose hands do not feel, pointing to the impotence of false gods. In Christ, the Word made flesh, God Himself engaged with humanity in the most tangible way, inviting us to a faith grounded in reality and relationship, not mere abstraction.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 27:21, Isaac says to Jacob, 'Come near, I pray thee, that I may feel thee, my son, whether thou be my very son Esau or not.' The use of מוּשׁ here emphasizes Isaac’s need for a physical, sensory confirmation of identity through touch. This moment reveals the human desire for certainty and the role of tangible proof in relationships, foreshadowing how God’s revelation often comes through concrete, personal encounters.
